explanations.explanation: Job does say those words, friend, but I think he is pouring on the sarcasm. Look at what comes right after: “But I also have a mind; I am not inferior to you.” (Job 12:3) Nobody follows up a real compliment like that. So the answer is False, and I think Job's tone says it all.

That's it, friend. I think Job is being sarcastic. Right after that line he says, “But I also have a mind; I am not inferior to you.” (Job 12:3) That's a man saying he can keep up just fine. He is not handing out trophies.

Job says, “I am a laughingstock to my friends, though I called on God, and He answered.” (Job 12:4) He says it twice, in fact, and adds that the righteous and upright man is a laughingstock. I think that stings, friend. It's one thing to be laughed at by strangers, and another to be laughed at by your own friends.
Job never says that, friend. He says he is a laughingstock to his friends, even though he called on God and God answered (Job 12:4). A teacher gets listened to. Job is getting laughed at.

Close, but no, friend. Job calls them “my friends,” and he says they treat him as a laughingstock (Job 12:4). A stranger would at least be polite. I think being laughed at by people you know is a different kind of sting.

Robbers is it. Job says, “The tents of robbers are safe, and those who provoke God are secure.” (Job 12:6) Think about how that sounds next to what he said about the righteous man. Job is saying the picture doesn't line up the way his friends keep telling him it does.

Not widows, friend. Job doesn't mention them here. He says, “The tents of robbers are safe, and those who provoke God are secure.” (Job 12:6) His point is that the wrong people look like they're doing fine.

Farmers don't show up in this verse, friend. Job says the tents of robbers are safe, and those who provoke God are secure (Job 12:6). He's saying the picture looks backwards to him. Honest work isn't the one getting the safe tent.

explanations.answer: The hand of the LORD has done this
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Job asks, “Which of all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this?” (Job 12:9) He sends his friends to the animals, the birds, the earth and the fish for it. The creatures are in on it, and Job is saying his friends should be too.

explanations.answer: The LORD has rested from His work
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend. Job never says that here. He says they all know “that the hand of the LORD has done this,” and the very next verse says the life of every living thing is in His hand (Job 12:9-10). That's not a God who stepped away.

explanations.answer: The LORD is far from His creatures
explanations.explanation: Job says the opposite, friend. Every creature knows that “the hand of the LORD has done this” (Job 12:9). Then he adds that the life of every living thing is in His hand (Job 12:10). A hand that holds your life is about as near as it gets.

That's the idea, friend. Job asks, “Does not the ear test words as the tongue tastes its food?” (Job 12:11) Your tongue checks before you swallow, and your ear should do the same. I think Job is hinting that his friends' words deserve a taste test.

explanations.answer: Repeat them to everyone they meet
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Job says the ear tests words, the way the tongue tastes its food (Job 12:11). Testing is the whole picture. Nothing in the verse says to pass them along.

explanations.answer: Forget them as soon as they hear them
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Job says, “Does not the ear test words as the tongue tastes its food?” (Job 12:11) Tasting means paying attention. You can't test something you've already forgotten.

God it is, friend. Job says, “Wisdom and strength belong to God; counsel and understanding are His.” (Job 12:13) He just said wisdom is found with the elderly (Job 12:12), and then he points higher. Long life is a good teacher, but God is where the wisdom comes from.

Kings come up later, friend, but not here. Job says, “Wisdom and strength belong to God; counsel and understanding are His.” (Job 12:13) Then he says God “loosens the bonds placed by kings” (Job 12:18). The crown is not where he says wisdom lives.

Priests show up a few verses later, friend, and not as the answer. Job says wisdom and strength belong to God (Job 12:13). Then he says God leads priests away barefoot (Job 12:19). Nobody in a robe is holding the wisdom.
True, friend. Job says, “If He holds back the waters, they dry up, and if He releases them, they overwhelm the land.” (Job 12:15) It goes both ways. The waters do what He lets them do.

Read that verse again, friend. Job says, “If He holds back the waters, they dry up, and if He releases them, they overwhelm the land.” (Job 12:15) So the statement on the card is True. Holding back or letting loose, the waters answer to Him.
Careful, friend, that card left something out. Job says, “The deceived and the deceiver are His.” (Job 12:16) That's both of them, not just one. So the statement is False.

Right, friend. Job says, “True wisdom and power belong to Him. The deceived and the deceiver are His.” (Job 12:16) Both are named, so “only the deceived” doesn't match. The verse doesn't leave out the deceiver.

Barefoot, friend. Job says, “He leads counselors away barefoot and makes fools of judges.” (Job 12:17) He says the same about priests in verse 19. I'd feel pretty small walking out of a big room without my shoes.
Chains aren't in these verses, friend. Job says God “leads counselors away barefoot” and “leads priests away barefoot” (Job 12:17, 19). It's the barefoot part that stings. No shoes, no dignity.

That would be a fancy exit, friend, and it's not what Job says. He says God “leads counselors away barefoot” and “leads priests away barefoot” (Job 12:17, 19). These folks are walking, and without shoes.
That's the picture, friend. Job says, “They grope in the darkness without light; He makes them stagger like drunkards.” (Job 12:25) No light, no reason, no map. Just a lot of wandering.

Not this crowd, friend. Job says they “grope in the darkness without light” and that He makes them “stagger like drunkards” (Job 12:25). There's no marching here. Nobody in that wasteland is keeping time.

Not quite, friend. Job says, “They grope in the darkness without light; He makes them stagger like drunkards.” (Job 12:25) Mourners walk with purpose, just slowly. These leaders are stumbling around with no path at all.

That's it, friend. Job says, “Yet I desire to speak to the Almighty and argue my case before God.” (Job 13:3) He's done going back and forth with his friends. I think he wants his answer from the One who actually has it.
Not quite, friend. Job says, “Yet I desire to speak to the Almighty and argue my case before God.” (Job 13:3) He doesn't want to disappear. He wants to talk, and to God Himself.

No more advice, friend. He's had plenty. Job says, “Yet I desire to speak to the Almighty and argue my case before God.” (Job 13:3) A few verses later he tells his friends to be silent so he can speak (Job 13:13).

Silence, friend. Job says, “If only you would remain silent; for that would be your wisdom!” (Job 13:5) That's the only wisdom he has left to offer them. It's a sharp line, and I think he means every word.
Job doesn't ask for gentler words, friend. He says, “If only you would remain silent; for that would be your wisdom!” (Job 13:5) He wants less talking, not softer talking.

Job isn't asking for a better speech, friend. He says, “If only you would remain silent; for that would be your wisdom!” (Job 13:5) More explaining is the last thing he wants. He'd rather hear nothing.
True, friend. Job says, “Surely He would rebuke you if you secretly showed partiality.” (Job 13:10) The word secretly is in there. Job is saying that hiding it from people won't hide it from God.
The text says otherwise, friend. Job says, “Surely He would rebuke you if you secretly showed partiality.” (Job 13:10) That makes the card's statement True. Keeping it secret doesn't change that.

That's the picture, friend. Job says, “Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay.” (Job 13:12) I think the idea is that ashes and clay don't hold up when pressed. Think of a cookie that crumbles the second you pick it up.

Job means the opposite, friend. He says, “Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay.” (Job 13:12) I think ashes and clay don't give you much to lean on. He isn't paying them a compliment.

explanations.answer: They are too deep to follow
explanations.explanation: Not deep, friend. Job says, “Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay.” (Job 13:12) Ashes and clay don't sound deep to me. I think he's calling their arguments flimsy.

Hope in Him, friend. Job says, “Though He slay me, I will hope in Him.” (Job 13:15) He knows speaking up is a risk, and he still keeps his hope with God. I think that's one of the boldest lines in the whole book.
Job isn't running anywhere, friend. He says, “Though He slay me, I will hope in Him.” (Job 13:15) He's already said he wants to speak to the Almighty (Job 13:3). Running is the opposite of that.
Job says the opposite, friend. He says, “Though He slay me, I will hope in Him.” (Job 13:15) Even with his life on the line, he doesn't give up on God. His hope stays right where it is.
True, friend. Job says, “I will still defend my ways to His face.” (Job 13:15) That comes in the same breath as his hope in God. He's holding both at once.

Look at the second half of that verse, friend. Job says, “Though He slay me, I will hope in Him. I will still defend my ways to His face.” (Job 13:15) So the card's statement is True. Job isn't backing down.

explanations.answer: That he is in the right
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. Job says, “See now, I have prepared my case; I know that I will be vindicated.” (Job 13:18) Vindicated means cleared. He's ready for his day in court, and he walks in sure of himself.
Job says the opposite, friend. He says, “I have prepared my case; I know that I will be vindicated.” (Job 13:18) A man who expects to be cleared isn't saying he earned his pain.
Quiet isn't his plan, friend. He says, “Be silent, and I will speak.” (Job 13:13) Then he says, “I have prepared my case; I know that I will be vindicated.” (Job 13:18) He's about to do some talking.
Not louder, friend. Job says, “Can anyone indict me? If so, I will be silent and die.” (Job 13:19) He says he'd go quiet if someone could prove a charge. So the card's statement is False.

That's it, friend. Job says, “Can anyone indict me? If so, I will be silent and die.” (Job 13:19) He doesn't say he'd argue louder. He says he'd be silent. I think that shows how sure he is of his case.
